plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to open a demat and trading account with a SEBI-registered broker, place a limit order for 1 share of a Nifty 50 company, read its price, market cap and P/E on a quote page, explain in one line why its price moved that day, and work out the tax you'd owe if you sold it.
plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14: you could compare two companies in the same sector using five numbers and say which you'd rather own and why.
plan.horizon28: Later, around day 28: you could have a written monthly plan splitting money between an index fund SIP and single shares, and one month of sticking to it.

picture.name: One big organised bazaar
picture.line: The Indian stock market is one huge organised bazaar: each company is a shop, a share is a tiny slice of ownership in one shop, and SEBI is the inspector who keeps the stalls honest.

chapters.title: A share is a slice of a shop
chapters.covers: What you actually own when you buy 1 share, and why its price moves every second: more buyers than sellers pushes it up, more sellers than buyers pushes it down.
chapters.outcome: You can explain in one line why a share's price rose or fell today using buyers and sellers, not headlines.

chapters.title: The two bazaars and their price boards
chapters.covers: NSE and BSE are the two exchanges (the market buildings), open 9:15 am to 3:30 pm Monday to Friday; Nifty 50 and Sensex are price boards for the 50 and 30 biggest shops; SEBI is the inspector.
chapters.outcome: You can read 'Nifty closed 0.8% down' and say what it does and does not tell you about the 50 companies behind it.

chapters.title: Your three accounts
chapters.covers: Bank account holds your money, trading account places orders through a broker, demat account is the locker (with NSDL or CDSL) that holds your shares; what KYC with PAN and Aadhaar means and what a broker charges.
chapters.outcome: You can open a demat and trading account and say which account holds your shares and which holds your cash.

chapters.title: Placing your first order
chapters.covers: Market order (buy now at any price) versus limit order (buy only at your price or better), choosing quantity, T+1 settlement meaning shares land the next working day, and the charges on one trade.
chapters.outcome: You can buy 1 share with a limit order, say when it lands in your demat, and list the charges you paid.

chapters.title: Reading a shop in five numbers
chapters.covers: Price, market cap (price times all shares, so the size of the shop), P/E (price divided by yearly profit per share, so how many years of profit you pay for), 52-week high and low, and dividend yield.
chapters.outcome: You can look at a quote page and say whether a company is large or small, and whether it is priced high or low against its profit.

chapters.title: Buying the whole bazaar at once
chapters.covers: Index funds buy all 50 Nifty shops in one go; mutual funds hire a shopper to pick for you; SIP means a fixed amount every month; expense ratio is the yearly fee taken from your money.
chapters.outcome: You can set up a monthly SIP in a Nifty 50 index fund and say what expense ratio you are paying.

chapters.title: The toll on the way out, and the traps
chapters.covers: Tax on listed shares: held under 12 months is taxed at 20%, held over 12 months at 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year; why to refuse stock tips, and why SEBI's 2023 study found 9 in 10 individual futures and options traders lost money.
chapters.outcome: You can work out the tax on a sale you are planning and name three things you will say no to in your first year.
